newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ mid-cap index makes inauspicious debut.
newsitem.headline: NZ mid-cap index makes inauspicious debut.

text.p: The New Zealand Stock Exchange's new Mid-cap stocks index made an inauspicious debut on Monday.
At 12.30 p.m. (0030 GMT) the Mid-Cap gross index was up 3.4 points to 2,617.6 while the capital index was up 1.6 at 1,835.1.
The index measures price trends of the 30 companies following the NZSE-10 in terms of market capitalisation, but excludes foreign companies and illiquid stocks.
Stocks must turn over 0.5 percent of their shares each month to be included, so tightly-held stocks such as Power New Zealand, New Zealand Refining and TransAlta are excluded.

NZSE chief executive Bill Foster told Reuters that while the exchange had no plans to launch a product based on the Mid-Cap such as the Tenz fund, there was a place for the index and at least one organisation does have plans.
"For some time we have had comment that the NZSE-40, which is our general markets index, is not all that easy to track -- some of the stocks are not so liquid down the bottom.
"It's not all that easy to replicate from a portfolio manager's point of view," Foster said.
"With the growing trend towards passive management and index management, people are looking for benchmark measures out in the market that they can replicate more easily," he said.
Foster said the exchange had received a listing application based on a Mid-cap index product.

The exchange was first to the draw last year with its passive Tenz product based on the top-10 index, which at the time attracted much publicity and some controversy because of its tax-free status. But Foster said other players were now
taking the initiative with their own products.
"If there is a gap in the market then the opportunity would be there for us to fill it."
Three fund managers spoken to by Reuters which have recently launched passive index funds had no plans to launch Mid-Cap based products.
Ord Minnett Equities Manager John Rattray said investor appetite for such funds had diminished substantially given the 10 percent fall of the NZSE-10 index this year.
"I wouldn't have thought the timing was great," he said of the launch of the Mid-cap index.
